# Pattern Interrupt Examples Video: 36 Hooks That Stop the Swipe

At 0:02, the creator looks into the camera, says “Today I’m sharing three gym tips,” and the viewer is already gone. The problem is not that the tips are useless. The opening gives the viewer no reason to interrupt the scroll.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This page gives you ready-to-use pattern interrupt examples for video, plus a simple way to choose one that fits your topic and test it without turning your first three seconds into noise.

## What a pattern interrupt does in a video

A pattern interrupt is an opening that breaks the viewer’s expectation: a surprising instruction, a specific mistake, a reversal, a visual reveal, or a question that creates a gap they want closed. It should lead directly into what your video can actually deliver.

The useful range is broad. A calm tutorial may need a precise “don’t do this first.” A comedy clip may need an absurd visual. A product demo may need the result before the method. The common job is the same: make the next second feel more valuable than the next swipe.

## Pattern interrupt examples for fitness videos

1. “Stop going to the gym every day.”
2. “The workout that made me quit was the ‘easy’ one.”
3. “If your first set looks like this, change it.”
4. “You do not need more motivation. You need a smaller first week.”
5. “This is why your [ADD: exercise] is not getting stronger.”
6. “I would not copy this viral workout.”
7. “Before you buy another supplement, watch this.”
8. “The hardest part of the gym happens before you touch a weight.”
9. “Most beginner plans fail on day [ADD: day number].”

## Pattern interrupt examples for beauty and style videos

10. “Put the expensive product down for a second.”
11. “This makeup step is making the rest of your face disappear.”
12. “I tried the trend on one side only.”
13. “Your concealer may be doing exactly what you asked it to do.”
14. “Do not choose your foundation shade under these lights.”
15. “The before is not the surprising part.”
16. “This outfit looked wrong until I changed one thing.”
17. “If your eyeliner keeps doing this, start here.”
18. “I used the same product two different ways. One was a mistake.”

## Pattern interrupt examples for food videos

19. “Do not preheat the pan yet.”
20. “This recipe starts with the part most people throw away.”
21. “I made the viral version so you do not have to.”
22. “The first bite is not why I keep making this.”
23. “Your [ADD: ingredient] is probably too cold.”
24. “This looks burned. It is supposed to.”
25. “The shortcut happens before you start cooking.”
26. “I changed one ingredient and the texture completely changed.”
27. “If dinner keeps becoming takeout, make this first.”

## Pattern interrupt examples for business, career, and creator videos

28. “Your portfolio is answering the wrong question.”
29. “Do not send that follow-up email yet.”
30. “This is the sentence that made my pitch harder to understand.”
31. “A busy calendar can hide this problem.”
32. “If a client says ‘I’ll think about it,’ listen for this.”
33. “I removed one slide before the meeting.”
34. “The advice to ‘post consistently’ leaves out this decision.”
35. “Your first line is not an introduction. It is a filter.”
36. “Before you film another talking-head video, choose this angle.”

## How to choose the right interruption

Start with the viewer’s existing assumption. Then choose the smallest honest break from it.

- Use a contrarian line when the video corrects a common habit: “Stop doing X.”
- Use a mistake line when you can show the error quickly: “This is why X fails.”
- Use a question when the answer is genuinely useful: “Why does X happen?”
- Use a visual mismatch when the image can carry the surprise before the spoken line.
- Use a result-first opening when you can show the finished outcome immediately, then explain the process.

Match the interruption to the payoff. If the hook says “don’t preheat the pan,” explain why within the next beat. If it says “stop going every day,” give the beginner-friendly alternative. A hook earns attention only when the video keeps its promise.

## A simple way to test pattern interrupts

Make three openings for the same video rather than making three different videos. Keep the topic, central lesson, and ending the same. Change only the first spoken line, on-screen text, and opening visual.

For example, a beginner gym video could test a contrarian opening, a question, and a mistake:

- Contrarian: “Stop going to the gym every day.”
- Question: “Why does everyone quit by January 20th?”
- Mistake: “You’re not lazy. You’re doing week one wrong.”

Watch the recordings with the sound off, then with the sound on. The first version needs a visual reason to pause; the second needs a spoken reason to keep listening. Keep the version that most clearly sets up the actual lesson, then refine the wording instead of adding bigger claims.

A pattern interrupt buys attention; a retention hook keeps it. See [retention hooks for Shorts](https://aniccaai.com/blog/retention-hooks-for-shorts?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=related_links_1101) for lines that carry viewers to the end.

## FAQ

### What makes a good pattern interrupt for video?

It is specific, understandable without context, and connected to the next part of the video. Surprise helps, but clarity is what carries the viewer into the explanation.

### Should every video start with a shocking statement?

No. A quiet contradiction, an unfinished result, or a close-up of the problem can interrupt a pattern without sounding dramatic. Choose the intensity that fits the audience and topic.

### Can I reuse the same hook format?

Yes. Reuse the structure, not the exact promise. “Stop doing X,” “You are not Y,” and “Before you do X” can each become a repeatable format when the specific insight changes.

### What should appear on screen during the hook?

Show the proof, problem, result, or action that makes the spoken line easier to understand. Keep on-screen text short enough to read during the opening beat.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the kind of brief and structured response it returns:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
